steps.say: This lesson shows the kernel's core: how a program asks the kernel for something, how processes and memory are kept, and the file system layer. The kernel follows the **Linux system call ABI**. Programs built for Linux ask for things in exactly the way Linux expects, so they run here unchanged.
A **system call** is a program asking the kernel to do something, such as read a file. The processor's `syscall` instruction lands here. The program's registers are saved in a frame and handed to C.

steps.anchor: /* Linux x86-64 system call numbers -> implementations. Numbers come from
steps.say: Each call has Linux's number: 0 is read, 1 is write, and so on. This one table lists every call the kernel has, about two hundred.

`syscall_dispatch` checks any seccomp filter (the sandbox rules a program may set on itself), calls the function for the number, puts the answer back in the program's register, and delivers any signal that is waiting.
A call that isn't there answers ENOSYS, "not implemented". The log says so once per call: `syscall N not implemented`. Look for that line when a new program misbehaves.
The calls themselves are grouped by subject: files in sys_fs.c, processes in sys_proc.c, memory in sys_mm.c, futex, epoll, inotify and the rest.
Each one is written with the SYSCALL macro: `SYSCALL(read)` defines `sys_read`, which takes six numbers, as Linux passes them, and returns the answer or a negative error.
A **process** is a running program. As in Linux it is a group of threads that share one address space (`mm`) and one table of open files (`fds`). Each thread has its own user_thread.

steps.say: The **scheduler** decides which thread runs on each processor core. It is preemptive: a thread is interrupted when its turn is up, even if it never yields.

steps.say: Each process has its own **address space**, its view of memory. Pages are given only when first touched. After fork, parent and child share pages until one of them writes, and only then is a copy made (copy-on-write).

steps.say: Touching a page that isn't there yet is a **page fault**, and it comes here. When memory runs out, the kernel first frees file pages it can read again, and only then ends a program to make room.

steps.say: The **VFS** (virtual file system) is the common layer every file system plugs into. Each one gives its files (vnodes) these operations. The comment above still says "ramfs now", but much more exists today.
These are what plug in: ramfs (files in memory), cpio (the boot archives), ext2 (the disk), procfs and sysfs (/proc and /sys), pipes, memfd and locks.

steps.say: The disk uses ext2 with ext3's journal. Changes are written to the journal first, so a power cut leaves the disk as it was before a batch or after it, never half done.
